title: The Earth and its Fullness
english: "They drink intoxicatingly by night." In darkness and ignorance, these people drink. But those who drink, having taken a divine drink—that is, having been made glad—drink in a sober way. "Eat, drink, be intoxicated, brothers," the Bridegroom says in the Song of Songs (Song of Songs 5:1). The "be intoxicated" does not mean this, not "be strengthened" from wine, but "be made glad."

And "your mercy shall pursue me all the days of my life" (Psalm 23:6). Your mercy is as if "I have anointed my head" (Psalm 23:5); it does not anoint my head for a little while, but always; since it is near to me, and thus every one of the anointed ones becomes a Christ eternally. Therefore "all the days of my life" pursues me; it does not allow me to become distant from it; for it is close by, since it is present to me, and thus every one of the anointed ones becomes a Christ eternally. It no longer dwells for a day or two, but for "all the days of my life." And "all the days of life" takes in the illuminations of the soul having come from the sun of righteousness.

A Psalm to David; of the first Sabbath. The superscription is appropriate; for it is for the one day of the Sabbaths. "One of the Sabbath"; the eighth following. This also is the first of the Sabbath. For since it is a beginning of a cycle of a week, it is also called the eighth; for the week is circumscribed up to the seventh, the seventh being an addition, that is, a day or a unit. The second begins again from a unit. This is called at one time the first of the Sabbath, that is, after the Sabbath, and at another time the eighth, so that the two weeks may be gathered together. In the giving of the holy part to the seven and the eight, the Jew alone has the Sabbath. They have neither the first of the Sabbath nor the eighth, having not at all considered the former week. Therefore, he alone, having the ecclesiastical opinion, who brings forth from his treasure new and old according to another comparison of the Gospel (Matthew 13:52), has the new of the Sabbath. Transcending the first week, he began the second, which is according to the Gospel. And this also is called the eighth in relation to the first week and the first of the Sabbaths.

The first verses of the Psalm can be understood both according to the word and the sense. But the fullness of the earth is to take in its world; for as Moses said: since plants and animals have come upon it, it is said: "it has been completed" (Genesis 2:1)...

The heavens and the earth. And God finished his works on the sixth day (Gen 2:2). We take this literally: that fruits and animals are the fullness of the earth. The apostle instructs, advising those from the Gentiles and the Jews not to be superstitious about foods, saying: 'Whatever is sold in the market, eat, without examining anything (1 Cor 10:25); for the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord (Ps 24:1).' Meat is especially sold in the markets, but also other things contributing to nourishment.

'The earth and its fullness belong to the Lord' (Ps 24:1) means the inhabited world and all who dwell in it. I said earlier that the earth was divided into its part for farming and its part for habitation. That which has the preparation for habitation is called the inhabited world, but that for farming and other things is called earth. God is the maker of both; for how could these be his, if he himself had not made them? Therefore, 'the earth and its fullness belong to the Lord' takes it in a general sense.

He established it upon the seas and prepared it upon rivers—that is, the earth or the inhabited world. The inhabited world is also the earth. What is said here is equal to what is said: 'He who made the earth stand upon the water,' and by Job: 'hanging the earth upon nothing' (Job 26:7); for if it is established in the sea, it does not have a hard and solid foundation, but in the waters it has the hanging. And every water has a ground beneath it. Since the sea has a ground beneath it, it must certainly have something underlying it. But nothing else is found except the liquid. For this reason, he says the earth is established upon the seas.

It holds itself by turning upon itself. It is not a hard ground supporting it as if so arranged, but it turns around itself. Indeed, even the Greeks say in their accounts that straight lines sent from a circle—and straight lines are not perceptible, but are considered by reason—hold it in the very center. And this is the hanging it upon nothing. This is the will of God; for 'you established the earth for its stability, it shall not be moved for ever and ever' (Ps 104:5). For how could the seat received by such a word of God be prone to falling? Since, therefore, the earth is upon the sea...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The misuse of reason and the metaphor of the soil
english: It has been founded, and a part of the earth is the inhabited world, and it itself appropriately has this seat by its moist nature. And he says regarding the rivers that it is prepared for them; not to be founded upon rivers, but to be prepared; for it is not possible to say that it has its foundation both in the sea and in the rivers, but it has been founded upon the sea, having been prepared for the rivers, so that it might be benefited by them, just as certain springs and channels flowing through it. Such bodies, if they do not have water sprinkled throughout them by which they can be held together, become fragments. And these things are [to be understood] regarding the literal sense.

But since the following things can no longer be taken historically: 'Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, and who shall stand in his holy place?' (Ps 24:3), it is necessary to say that the way of the ascent and the seat of the standing were not mentioned, but the answer is made to the one asking: 'Who is the one ascending and who is the one standing?' Thus: 'innocent of hands and pure in heart.' That being innocent refers to the hands, and that being pure refers to the actions. Then he says 'a divine character': 'innocent of hands and pure in heart, who has not taken his soul in vain.'

This is understood in two ways. 'In vain' refers to the foolish person taking his own soul, deliberating, choosing, and acting; for often these things—the unseemly, the sensible, the transitory—are signified by the name 'vain'; as if he were saying, 'and you will know where you were, when you were trusting in vain things,' meaning the transitory things. It can also refer to the sins themselves. 'In vain' he took [it], the one rising in the morning and drinking wine and staying late so as to be consumed by the wine; for 'woe to those who rise early and pursue strong drink and stay late; for the wine will consume them' (Isa 5:11). Again, they have haste to rise from dawn and hurry to the courts, in which injustice follows; this one 'has taken his soul in vain.' This is also consistent with what is said in Isaiah to certain people: 'Vain is the strength of your spirit' (Isa 5:12). Here, 'spirit' is the opinion. Similarly, this applies to what was said concerning the Virgin, that just as she is holy in body, so she is holy in spirit, in opinion and in mind. Therefore, 'vain' is 'the strength of your spirit.' If anyone, then, [uses] the mind...

His mind is also worn out by 'worldly cares' toward vain things; his strength is in vain. They exhaust the power of reasoning toward vain things. Indeed, one can see such people and even more wicked ones. They exhaust the whole strength of the mind toward these things.

A second explanation for: 'who has not received his soul in vain' (Psalm 39:9). God prepared man as a rational being, not merely so that he might possess reasoning and do nothing according to it; for this He made the rational being, so that he might receive virtue and exercise it. 'He has received his soul in vain' does not mean God gave it thus, but that he himself has taken it thus. As one might say, for example: He made man from soul and body, and there are certain movements of the soul, and there are also movements of the body. We have the activity of members: walking, doing something with the hands, seeing. If anyone, then, for instance, having feet, never walks, he has his feet 'in vain' in a certain way.

And for an upward leading: the following [words] force even the preceding verses to be led upward. 'The Lord' is that 'earth,' that 'good and noble heart' which received the one whom Jesus cast seed, and bore fruit a hundredfold, or a hundred and sixty and thirty (Matthew 13:8). Often I have said that the intelligible things can be taken in the same way through more various thoughts, when they were saying the soul is a sheep and a plant. Here, therefore, the same earth is both earth and inhabited world. When, therefore, it bears the practical virtues, it is an earth having fullness. But when it has the divine gifts of the Spirit, it is an inhabited world having inhabitants. It is not a desert; for He has not said, 'Come, and let us abandon it,' as it is said to the doomed inhabited world. And this is the assembly of the Jews.

And he extends this also to every soul having, at first, a dwelling, but leaving it by its own fault. Therefore, this is connected to: 'He himself founded it upon the seas' (Psalm 74:3). Sea and seas is the name given to the place of earth and the condition of those dwelling there. Having being in billows and in saltiness, I call the dwelling; upon these seas He founded it. And this sea takes the sting of Jesus, so that from it...

title: The Integrity of Oaths and the Source of Blessing
english: Let the diligent catch good animals. But if these hunters are friends of virtue, they are said to be hunted from the sea so that they may come out of it, and in another way to be established upon the sea; for here they are established so that they may appear 'having been rooted and built up in love' (Eph 3:17). And 'upon the rivers' (Ps 46:4) of those flowing from the belly of the one having the Spirit, they are prepared, so that they may receive these rivers flowing from the belly of each believer. And the various gifts of the Spirit are the rivers.

For the one wishing to learn toward the one being examined: 'Who is he that ascends into the mountain of the Lord and stands in the holy place?' (Ps 24:3). An answer is brought: 'You seek who is ascending and standing? He who is innocent with his hands and pure in heart, who has not taken his soul in vain' (Ps 24:4).' This is the one ascending through progress. And progress is the ascent. And the standing is in the perfection. When someone becomes 'perfect as the Father in heaven' (Matt 5:48), he has stood in the holy place, unless indeed he surpasses the whole such state and takes the beginning of another; therefore also in the psalms it is said: 'I have seen the end of every completion' (Ps 37:36).

There are many ends, as it is in the learning of letters. One completes the task in the knowledge of the characters, and begins by syllabifying, and again, having attained the end of those, a different beginning becomes. For a circle, one cannot take either a beginning or an end. If, therefore, one recognizes from a sign the beginning of the circle, and completes the whole circle, he comes again to the beginning, as it is with the sun. In such things, ends are always brought according to the same pattern.

The Jews, therefore, perhaps say that 'to ascend to the mountain' means to ascend into the temple and to stand in it. The following things are gathered together by this thought. 3–4 Who shall ascend into the mountain of the Lord and who shall stand in his holy place? Innocent with hands and pure in heart, who has not taken his soul in vain and has not sworn in vain to his neighbor. It lies in the Decalogue: 'You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain; for the Lord will not cleanse him who takes his name in vain' (Ex 20:7). This must be grasped inwardly, perfectly, introductory, and appropriately by those beginning. Chiefly the...

The young man, being ready to receive the laws of God, 'does not swear at all' (Matt 5:37); therefore he does not take the name of the Lord in vain. He receives it not in vain, being satisfied with 'yes, yes' and 'no, no' (Matt 5:37). It is possible for those introducing this to say: it is not necessary to swear falsely; for he who falsely invokes the name of the Lord, as far as it reaches him, has received it in vain; since he is able to demonstrate even faith to the one disputing, and easily brings him to the oath without an oath. This faith through an oath they call unprovable.

And the external laws, when it was not possible to demonstrate, not through writings, not through witnesses—then also he does not cast himself upon swearing, but the judges, desiring to find every proof and not finding it, flee to this last resort. 'Who did not take his soul in vain' (Ps 15:4). And immediately he joined: 'nor did he swear upon deceit' (Ps 15:4); for everyone swears 'upon deceit' perversely; for he does not think he is swearing perversely. It rarely happens through ignorance. Often someone, forgetting, swears, and again there is an accusation, as regarding sins committed while unheard.

I say: some do not blame those who are drinking while saying what should not be said, and doing what is not necessary, saying that drunkenness is an unconscious state by which these things which they are blamed for happen after drinking; but drunkenness itself is voluntary; for it was necessary not to get drunk.

This one shall receive a blessing from the Lord. Having outlined who is the one ascending the mountain and standing in a holy place, and what follows such a person, he says: according to the one who ascended, he is in the mountain of God and standing in a holy place. And after the ascent of the mountain, so that the summit of the mountain may be the holy place, he says that 'this one shall receive a blessing from the Lord', 'a spiritual blessing, the one in the heavens'; for it is said: 'for indeed the Lawgiver will give blessing'. And the Lawgiver gives not to those transgressing the law, but to those turning toward it in deed. And again: 'Behold, thus', he says, 'shall be blessed the man who fears the Lord' (Ps 128:1). The cause of the blessing is reverence, the fear toward the Lord; therefore it is said: 'The Lord shall bless you out of Zion' (Ps 128:5). If God blesses such a person from Zion, because of virtue having preceded him and right understanding for him...
